title: Forecasting suitable areas for wind turbine occurrence to proactively improve wildlife conservation
abstract: The United States is rapidly expanding production of renewable energy to meet increased energy demands and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Wind energy is at the forefront of this transition. A central challenge is un­ derstanding the nexus between wind energy development and its capacity for negative effects on wildlife causing population declines and habitat loss. Collaboration among conservationists and developers, early in the planning process, is crucial for minimizing wind-wildlife conflicts. Such collaborations require data showing where wind and wildlife impacts occur. To meet this challenge and inform decision-making, we provide natural resource agencies and stakeholders information regarding where future wind turbines may occur, and the potential affects on natural resource management, including the conservation of priority species and their habitats. We developed a machine learning model predicting suitability of wind turbine occurrence (hereafter, wind turbine suitability) across an eight-state region in the United States, representing some of the richest areas of wind potential. Our model incorporates predictor variables related to infrastructure, land ownership, meteorology, and topography. We additionally created a constraint layer indicating areas where wind would likely not be developed because of zoning, protected lands, and restricted federal agency proximity guidelines. We demonstrate how the predictive wind turbine suitability model informs conservation planning by incorporating animal movement models, relative abundance models coupled with spatial conservation planning software, and population density models for three exemplar, high priority species often affected by wind energy: whooping cranes (Grus americana), golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos), and lesser prairie-chickens (Tympanuchus pallidicinctus). By merging the wind turbine and biological models, we identified conservation priority areas (i.e., places sharing high suitability for wind turbines and species use), and places where wind expansion could minimally affect these species. We use our “species-wind turbine occurrence relationships” to demonstrate applications, illustrating how forecasting areas of wind turbine suitability promotes wildlife conservation. These relationships inform wind energy siting to reduce negative ecological impacts while promoting environmental and economic viability.

## **1. Introduction**

The global energy sector continues emphasizing renewable sources of energy to stem greenhouse gas emissions (Field et al., 2014; Audoly et al., 2018; Sawin et al., 2018), making renewables the fastest growing energy technology with onshore wind energy being one of the leaders in market penetration (Murdock et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020; USEIA, 2021). Presently, wind energy comprises more than 9% of the United

States electricity generation from over 70,000 operational turbines providing more than 140 GW of energy capacity (Wiser et al., 2022; USEIA, 2023). By midcentury, wind energy could reach 404 GW, contributing ~ 35% of the nation’s energy production (USDOE, 2015). Though climate change requires immediate actions, the biodiversity crisis is not the same thing as the climate crisis and is no less serious (Koh et al., 2004; Field et al., 2014). Landscape scale, ecological changes occur with any type of energy development, with the construction and

Indeed, numerous studies demonstrate the adverse consequences wind energy can engender to species, ecosystems, trophic dynamics, and biodiversity (Evans & Kiesecker, 2014; Fernandez-Bellon et al., 2019; Thaker et al., 2018; Allison  ́ et al., 2019; Diffendorfer et al., 2019; Rehbein et al., 2020). Proactive planning is crucial to ensure the projected environmental impacts of this rapid projected growth in wind energy are mitigated (Straka et al., 2020). Ideally, conversations between conservationists and stakeholders should occur during the siting process. Such actions can benefit from data identifying areas suitable for wind turbines and wind power production that are also valuable for wildlife, to inform wind energy siting and pre-emptively avoid wind development in biologically sensitive areas.

Previous studies have made advances in hypothesizing scenarios for future build out and capacity expansion of wind energy (Mai et al. 2021). Existing resources, such as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory’s (NREL) Wind Integration National Dataset Toolkit and Wind Prospector (Draxl, Hodge et al., 2015; Draxl, Clifton et al., 2015) and NREL’s powerful economic-based resource capacity and potential models (Regional Energy Deployment System Model, Ho et al., 2021; and The Renewable Energy Potential Model, Maclaurin et al., 2019) can assist with determining new integration of renewable energy technologies and optimal build out given grid infrastructure and land use. There are also federal voluntary siting guidelines to aid in avoidance of harm to wildlife populations, namely eagles (USFWS, 2012). Furthermore, some studies have used spatial and non-spatial multicriteria decisions approaches to determine where renewable energy may be developed in the future (Janke, 2010; Miller and Li, 2014). Other studies have focused more of wind-wildlife conflicts, such as predicted areas of probable mortality of bats by relating environmental characteristics at existing wind farms to location of bat mortality (Santos et al., 2013), predicting wind turbine risk to eagles inferred from paired resource selection models (Miller et al., 2014), and assessment of ecological sensitivities of deployment of renewable technologies (Gove et al., 2016). A more recent study mapped wind resources while incorporating development constraints important wildlife habitat to determine areas where sufficient wind resources occur and the energy production capacity of these areas (Hise et al., 2022). These past studies and available resources offer valuable information to determine renewable energy potential and inform the siting process and several go a step further and place these factors within a conservation context. An extension of this body of research is directly linking predictions of locations suitable for future wind turbines, as opposed for example to wind energy potential, and important wildlife areas. Such a product would allow for quantification of the ecologically or biologically sensitive areas that may be faced with future development while concomitantly identifying potential areas suitable for wind turbines but unimportant to wildlife.

Predicting locations suitable for wind turbines is not a trivial exercise, however, the results can promote the identification of areas that may be developed and have minimal impact to wildlife. The reason this type of modelling approach is challenging is likely due to the complexities associated with the siting of wind turbines which is dependent on optimization of the physical characteristics and meteorological conditions of a site (i.e., where wind turbines are being prospected to be built), the existing infrastructure and access to the energy grid, federal and state ordinances and regulations, national security risks, aeronautical hazards, social acceptance, and profitability (USDOE, 2008; Evans & Kiesecker, 2014; Behera et al., 2015; Tegen et al., 2016; Cetinay et al., 2017; FAA, 2018; Thomas et al., 2018; Haac et al., 2019; Hoen et al., 2019). Furthermore, to predict areas of future suitability for wind turbines, variables influencing siting ideally would be statistically quantifiable and produce spatially explicit predictions for assessing an areas suitability for wind turbines to help meet social, economic, and environmental criteria. Such a novel statistical methodology would

build upon previous studies investigating wind energy development and further lend a powerful resource to practical conservation measures by providing additional decision support to evaluate sites highly suitable for supporting wind turbines and spatially congruent with important wildlife populations and habitat.

To meet this need and advance nature conservation, we derived a robust dataset to formulate a machine learning model predicting an area’s suitability for wind turbine placement (hereafter wind turbine suitability). More specifically, the model predicts the probability an area is suitable to support wind turbines based of a collection of features (e.g., physical, cultural characteristics) contained within that area. We additionally leveraged the distribution of wildlife populations, their movements, and habitats with predictions describing the suitable areas for wind turbines. Analyses of these data reveal where possible future conflicts may exist between wind development and wildlife. Identification of high priority conservation areas motivate important conversations between natural resource agencies and proposed wind projects regarding the development of areas that have habitat or population significance for wildlife. Places ill-suited for wildlife with potential for wind turbine suitability form ideal targets for wind siting and should be incentivized.

To test the utility of our framework we demonstrate how 1) animal movement models, 2) relative abundance models coupled with spatial conservation planning software, and 3) population density models can be combined with the wind turbine suitability model to identifying important habitat and population distribution estimates for three priority species as it relates to the potential occurrence of wind turbines. We selected whooping cranes ( _Grus americana_ ), golden eagles ( _Aquila chrysaetos_ ) and lesser prairie-chickens ( _Tympanuchus pallidicinctus_ ), as these species cover a spectrum of volitant long-distance migratory, resident migratory and terrestrial birds to exemplify the application of the wind turbine suitability model.

The aims of our analyses are twofold. We provide natural resource agencies with information describing where potential future wind turbines may occur and how this development overlaps with resource needs of priority species. Subsequently, these results inform conservation prioritization and planning, to assist wind energy projects early in the siting and planning process by minimizing impacts the development may have on species of concern, while maximizing the other important environmental and economic returns inherent to wind energy production.

## **2. Methods**

## _2.1. Study Area_

We studied wind energy development across several regions of the United States. Specifically, we predicted wind turbine suitability in Arizona, Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Texas and southern portions of Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, and Mississippi. These states support major wind energy development in the southwestern United States, portions of the northern and southern Great Plains, and portions of the Gulf Coast (Fig. 1). Currently, approximately 50% of electricity produced from wind energy in the United States comes from these states (WINDExchange, 2023).

## _2.2. Wind data derivation_

We examined variables influencing the siting and placement of wind turbines and associated facilities. We used the U.S. Geological Survey Wind Turbine Database to identify the geographical locations for current wind turbines (Hoen et al., 2018). Characteristics at wind turbine sites likely represent suitable conditions and capture the variation in conditions at wind turbines that have been built across the study area. We associated the locations of turbines with variables within four categories to capture current conditions at wind turbines: 1) metrological, 2)

The U.S. National Grid (https://usngcenter.org) served as our reference system, with each 1 km[2 ] grid cell forming an experimental unit. We identified if 0 or ≥ 1 wind turbine(s) occurred in each cell and calculated statistics for each predictor variable described below within that cell.

## _2.3. Meteorological data_

We compiled metrological variables from the Wind Integration National Dataset Toolkit (Draxl, Clifton et al., 2015) that are relevant for evaluating wind power resources across the United States. The meteorological dataset was calculated with the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (Skamarock and Klemp, 2008) and numerical weather prediction models over a 2 km[2 ] point grid spanning the continental Unites States (Draxl, Hodge et al., 2015). The models simulated metrological conditions at each grid point at hourly intervals. Each annual dataset is open access and was downloaded from Amazon Simple Storage Service buckets which are cloud-based storage systems. These datasets contained hourly estimates of each metrological variable within our study area. We selected the most recent 5 years of the simulated dataset (2010–2014) to estimate average hourly values for each meteorological variable at varying altitudes (Table 1). ## _2.5. Infrastructure_

We accounted for current infrastructure required for supporting wind energy development, by compiling datasets that identify established transmission lines and road networks throughout the study area. For transmission lines, we used data from the Homeland Infrastructure Foundation Level Data (USDHS, 2020) and a transmission lines database (S&P Global Platts). We derived a roads layer containing all primary and secondary roads in the study (USCB, 2019a; GeoFabrik, 2020). We calculated total length and total number of unique transmission lines and roads in each 1 km[2 ] grid cell to approximate the configuration and composition of these infrastructure features.

## _2.6. Land ownership data_

Additionally, we used the U.S. Bureau of Land Management (USBLM 2019) national surface management agency database to acquire surface land ownership across the study area. Categories of land ownership included public, private, military, Tribal, and an “other” category. We estimated areal proportion of each land ownership category within each 1 km[2 ] grid cell.

## _2.7. Areas of wind turbine exclusion and derivation of exclusion layer_

We complied spatial data related to siting guidelines to identify areas within the study area where wind development is unlikely to occur given zoning and ordinance restrictions, protected lands, aeronautical hazards, and national security (i.e., exclusion areas). We used the U.S. Geological Survey Protected Areas Database of the United States (PADUS, U.S. Geological Survey Gap Analysis Project, 2020) and identified all areas with GAP Protection Status Code of 1 or 2 (indicating protection of biological resources, Evans & Kiesecker, 2014) as unavailable for wind development. We also confirmed that we included protected lands in the PADUS that were unclassified with GAP Status Codes in PADUS (e.g., state parks, wildlife management areas, preserves, conservation easements, etc.). We excluded areas from wind turbine placement with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) special use airspace with designations of alert areas, prohibited areas, and restricted areas. We excluded class B airspace (busiest airports in the United States). Furthermore, we excluded areas within a 3 km buffer of runways and helipads from wind turbine development (USDOE, 2008; Hise et al., 2022) and urban areas (locations having ≥ 50000 people USCB, 2019b). Finally, areas within 3 km of Next Generation Weather Radar (NEXRAD) and Terminal Doppler Weather Radar stations and 9.26 km of Department of Defense Long Range Radar stations were excluded from wind turbine placement (Tegen et al., 2016; FAA, 2018; Hise et al., 2022). Weather radar station data was sourced from the Homeland Infrastructure Foundation Level Data (USDHS, 2020). We combined all these spatial data to create a single polygon layer representing exclusion areas.

## _2.8. Data analysis_

A conceptual workflow provides clarification of our entire analytical approach (Fig. 2). We applied machine learning to model the occurrence (i.e., presence and absence of wind turbines within a 1 km[2 ] grid cell) of wind turbines in relation to the explanatory variables (Table 1) to predict conditions suitable to support wind turbines across the study area (i. e., probability of wind turbine occurrence). We implemented random forest classification techniques which uses a modified forward selection procedure and apply to data of high dimensionality, and situations where polynomial regression and nonparametric procedures are needed to describe the complex interactions and nonlinear relationships between explanatory variables and the response variables (Breiman, 2001; Cutler et al., 2007). Random forests models use an ensemble of decision trees to construct a deterministic forest by averaging predictions across trees. Random forests employ bagging where multiple classification or regression tree models are independently fit with a bootstrap training data sample with replacement, leaving ~ 1/3 aside for testing each tree (i.e., “out-of-bag samples”). These out-of-bag-samples are used to estimate out-of-bag error by seeing how well the predictive model predicts the test data. Model predictions are made by a simple majority vote (Breiman, 2001). The random forest decision trees-based algorithms can generate higher prediction accuracy than traditional parametric approaches (Cutler et al., 2007; Crisci et al., 2012; Cushman & Wasserman, 2018; Dobrini ́c et al., 2021). We used a probability random forest classification model, a modification of the random forest algorithm for predicting class probabilities (Malley et al., 2012; Messager et al., 2021), to predict probability of wind turbine occurrence or predicted suitable condition of wind resources to support wind turbines. We used the R package _ranger_ version 0.12.0 (Wright & Ziegler, 2015) to implement the model.

We emphasize model predictions. Given the large number of variables, we used principal components analysis to reduce data dimensionality. Since we were not concerned with the data generating process _per se_ , and to avoid potential issues with multicollinearity and overfitting the models, we employed a modified rotation forest approached proposed by Rodriguez et al., (2006). The principal components explaining most of the variation and their rotated values (i.e., scores) became the predictor variables. Because our data was inherently zero inflated (i.e., most grid cells had zero turbines present) we used a random undersampling design to avoid issues with sample imbalances which can result in poor model performance for machine learning techniques (Japkowicz & Stephen, 2002; Kuhn & Johnson, 2013; Ng et al., 2014; Hounkpatin et al., 2018). We tested several undersampling ratios for the training dataset and determined that randomly selecting equal number of samples (i.e., records) with turbines absent to turbines present resulted in sufficiently balancing the samples and avoided model overfitting.

Parameter optimization is important in tree-based machine learning techniques to ensure accurate predictions. To tune the model parameters, we used the R package tuneRanger version 0.5 (Probst et al., 2019) and out of bag predictions from the random forest model to determine

optimal values for the three hyperparameters, minimum node size (minimum number of observations within a terminal node), sample fraction (number of observations drawn for training each tree) and mtry (number of randomly drawn candidate predictor variables). We used Briers score to assess hyperparameter optimization for the classification model. We also used the R package caret version 6.0–92 (Kuhn et al., 2020) to employ 5-fold cross validation and ran 100 iterations to determine the optimal number of trees to include in the random forest models, given classification accuracy and Kappa statistics, generating a total of 500 estimates for each performance metric.

We also used 5-fold cross validation and ran 100 iterations to assess the predictive performance of the model. For each iteration, we randomly subsampled the dataset to match the equal ratio of samples with and without turbines to ensure stability in classification predictions across multiple random sampling instances. For each iteration, we estimated a total of 500 estimates for multiple accuracy metrics including Classification Accuracy, Area Under the Curve (AUC), Kappa Statistic and Sensitivity and Specificity to evaluate predictive performance.

The USGS Wind Turbine Database is updated quarterly, providing an opportunity to measure our model’s ability to predict the suitability of areas where new turbines were built. Since new turbines were built in the subsequent quarterly update that were not included as inputs of the response variable, we compared the suitability values from our prediction to these newly built areas. Additionally, we validated the model with prospected sites that have undergone FAA obstruction evaluation. In accordance with 14 CFR Part 77.9, any proposed construction of wind turbines must have an aeronautical study and obtain a determination from the FAA confirming no aeronautical hazard for the site, and builders must file notice with the FAA at least 45 days prior to beginning construction. We subset the FAA’ s digital obstacle file, to include prospected sites lacking turbine construction (i.e., no built date associated with the record of the study) and not deemed hazardous to aeronautical safety. These sites suggest areas suitable for turbine development yet remain unbuilt. To ensure these sites were vacant and remained undeveloped (i.e., not recording or updating errors), we calculated the distance between each built turbine to the nearest built turbine, and the minimum of these nearest distances within the entire study area. We then calculated the distance between the purported unbuilt sites and the nearest built turbine and only included unbuilt sites having distances greater than the minimum distance between all the built turbines. We overlaid both newly built turbines and determined unbuilt sites on the wind turbine suitability predictions and extracted the probability values to create frequency distributions to determine if our model was sufficiently predicting wind turbine suitability at these sites.

We used the U.S. Geological Survey YETI high performance computer cluster (Falgout & Gordon, 2017) to process data and calculate zonal statistics. We used the _spatialEco_ package version 1.3–7 in R to calculate zonal statistics (Evans & Murphy, 2020) and _raster_ package version 3.5–21 in R (Hijmans et al., 2015) for raster creation and interpolation. All spatial processing and analyses and statistical analyses were conducted in ArcGIS Pro 2.3.0 (ESRI, 2019), QGIS 3.26.0 (QGIS Development Team, 2020), and R 4.1.2 (R Core Team, 2020). The spatial resolution of all derived raster data and wind turbine suitability model predictions were 30 m[2 ] and 1 km[2] , respectively.

## _2.9. High profile species case studies_

## _2.9.1. Golden eagles_

Under the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act, and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, golden eagles are a federally protected species. In the United States, golden eagles experience mortality from collisions with wind turbines (Pagel et al., 2013; New et al., 2015). Much of golden eagle seasonal habitat, especially during migration, occurs where current wind turbines exist, which elevates collision risks (Katzner et al., 2017; Ruiz-Gutierrez et al., 2021; New et al. 2021). To promote the

environmental and economic benefits of wind energy production while reducing negative affects to eagle populations, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service implements a permitting process allowing “take” or incidental fatalities of eagles from collisions with wind turbines (USFWS Service, 2012).

We used the predictive wind turbine suitability model to locate areas that could support turbines and have high relative abundance of golden eagles throughout its annual cycle. We used eBird relative abundance estimates of golden eagles generated by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology to determine the relative abundance of golden eagles in the prebreeding, breeding, post-breeding and non-breeding seasons (Fink et al., 2020). These data are publicly available (https://science.ebird.

org/en/status-and-trends/species/goleag/downloads?week=1).

Random forest models were used to estimate seasonal relative abundance of golden eagles. Citizen science data (i.e., eBirder bird observations) formed the response variable. The models contain covariates such as elevation, topography, and habitat. Models were optimized for sampling, search effort and weather conditions to improve accounting for sources of variation related to the detection process (Fink et al. 2020).

We used the Zonation v.4 conservation planning software (Moilanen, 2007; Moilanen et al., 2014) to form an assessment of the spatial landscape priorities given the four seasonal periods of golden eagle relative abundance and the predictions from the wind turbine suitability model. Zonation algorithms produces a ranking of the landscape, where the top 1% of planning units (i.e., pixels) is nested within the top 2%, 5%, 10%, and 25% (least conservation value) of the landscape while ensuring habitat connectivity and unit importance to multiple species or multiple seasons. The rankings consider the contributions of seasonal relative abundance of golden eagles, which is conditional on the wind turbine suitability predictions and what areas remain on the landscape. We masked all data to the study area and ensured extent and rows and columns of each of the five rasters were consistent prior to the running in Zonation. We used the core-area cell removal rule, a warp factor of 100, and an edge removal of 1. Weights in Zonation are relative among the input layers. To emphasize the equal importance of golden eagle abundance across all seasons in the Zonation analysis we included a species weight of 1.5 for each golden eagle relative abundance for each season and a conditional weight of 0.5 for the wind turbine suitability layer (Early & Thomas, 2007) to identify priority conservation areas for golden eagles in the context of wind turbine suitability. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service previously determined that a map layer consisting of all cells that had an eBird relative abundance value in the upper 70% of the relative abundance distribution in any season included _>_ 90% of known golden eagle nest sites across the conterminous western U.S. using the same approach as described in Ruiz-Gutierrez et al. (2021). Therefore, the eBird relative abundance threshold was known to be protective of golden eagle nesting habitat. We selected 70% as the cutoff for high versus low conservation priority for golden eagles.

## _2.9.2. Whooping cranes_

Whooping cranes are an endangered and federally protected species. The Aransas Wood Buffalo Population of whooping cranes migrate from their breeding grounds near the Northwest Territories, Canada, to their wintering grounds along the Texas Gulf Coast, USA. During their migration whooping cranes traverse the North American Great Plains and typically avoid wind turbines they encounter along their migration, which can influence their habitat use and bioenergetics (Pearse et al., 2021). Furthermore, there is increased concern that future development of wind energy throughout their range could result in habitat loss (i.e., avoided areas) and increase crane mortality in the form of collisions with overhead power or with the turbines themselves. Increased mortality could reduce population growth and impact species recovery (CWS and USFWS, 2007; Butler, Metzger et al., 2017; Pearse et al., 2021). We used GPS locations from whooping cranes tagged with satellite transmitters from 2009 to 2018 (Pearse et al., 2020). These data are publicly available (https://www.sciencebase.

gov/catalog/item/5ea3071582cefae35a19349a). To estimate whooping crane space use along their migration corridor and integrate this information with predicted wind turbine suitability we estimated population level utilization distributions. We used the biased random bridge estimator to estimate utilization distributions of whooping cranes (Benhamou and Corn ́elis, 2010). This approach considers the sampling interval of GPS locations thereby accounting for spatial autocorrelation. The biased random bridge approach considers both advection, or a drift component, and the diffusive movement of Brownian motion thus incorporating an animal’s propensity to move in the direction of the subsequent GPS location but also in other directions of the drift component resulting in a more realistic animal movement model (Benhamou and Corn ́elis, 2010; Lei et al., 2019). We used the adehabitatHR package version 0.4.19 in R to estimate the biased random bridge models (Calenge, 2011). We considered birds with ≥ 70 locations within one migration event as eligible for the analysis as we could not accurately estimate a utilization distribution with fewer locations. We also removed any locations that had inaccuracies related to duplicative or anomalous GPS fixes present in the data (refer to location filter descriptions in metadata for GPS locations of whooping cranes). We set the gird cell size at 1 km[2 ] and used the plug-in method for the diffusion coefficient, 100 m for the minimum smoothing parameter and 60 sec for the interpolation time for parametrizing the biased random bridge function. We summed utilization distributions of all whooping cranes during the fall and spring migration and standardized the summed utilization distribution values, so the pixel values ranged from 0 to 100. We used the 99% volume contour to define the population level utilization distribution for whooping cranes during fall and spring migration (Lei et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2020). Once the population level utilizations were defined, we multiplied both the spring and fall migration utilization distributions with the wind turbine suitability predictions to determine the joint probability of intensity of use and wind turbine suitability. We considered areas with the highest joint probabilities as high conservation priority areas.

## _2.9.3. Lesser Prairie-Chickens_

Wind energy development in the Great Plains is projected to expand due to energy demands in the United States (AWEA, 2019), affecting the conservation of the threatened (Northern Distinct Population Segment) and endangered (Southern Distinct Population Segment) lesser prairiechickens and other grassland obligate species requiring intact grasslands (Garton et al., 2016; Nasman et al., 2018; USFWS, 2021). The consequences of wind turbines, and the necessary infrastructure for operation, on lesser-prairie chickens is not well understood. There may, however, be negative behavioral and demographic responses by prairie grouse to wind energy development including avoidance (i.e., displacement), increased predation risk due to required overhead transmission lines, habitat loss, and fragmentation (Pruett et al., 2009; Walters et al., 2014; LeBeau et al., 2020; USFWS, 2021).

Population density, when accounting for environmental variables that reflect habitat characteristics, can be used to establish population density-habitat relationships to reveal areas on the landscape most important to a species (Royle et al., 2004; Butler, Sesnie et al., 2017; Guisan et al., 2017). We replicated the procedures outlined Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017) with updated covariables to estimate density of lesser prairie-chickens in New Mexico and Texas, USA. Timmer et al. (2014) established a sampling frame of survey blocks in Texas of 12.96 km[2 ] and flew aerial surveys between 2010 and 2011 along transects counting groups of lesser prairie-chickens within each block (see Timmer et al., 2014; Butler, Metzger et al., 2017, Butler, Sesnie et al., 2017 for survey design and survey protocol). Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017) estimated spatially explicit density of lesser prairie-chickens in Texas using hierarchical distance sampling (Royle et al., 2004; Sillett et al., 2012) with covariates related to landcover, land surface phenology, as well as human infrastructure and topography. The specific land surface phenology covariables used by Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017) were no longer curated by USGS and replaced with a newer land surface

phenology dataset. Thus, to use the model created by Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017) to predict contemporary lesser prairie-chicken group densities, we refit the model using the new covariables. We updated the covariables for oil and gas development, road density, land surface phenology, and landcover (Table 2) following the methodology detailed in Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017). We refit models using the new covariables measured at the time of the survey, used the procedures outlined in Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017) to select the best model based on Akaike’s Information Criterion (AIC; Anderson & Burnham, 2004), and predicted and biascorrected density using the new covariables measured in 2007–2021 (Table 2). For our study, we predicted and bias-corrected density to survey blocks in eastern New Mexico where surveys were not conducted. Derivation of the covariates and statistical approach followed the same procedure outlined in Butler, Sesnie et al. (2017). We normalized the density estimates of lesser prairie-chicken groups to range from 1 (highest density) to 0 (lowest density). We overlaid the scaled density estimates on the wind turbine suitability predictions and multiplied the density by the mean wind turbine suitability estimates within each quadrat. This approach enabled identifying of areas where lesser prairiechicken populations and wind turbine suitability coincide.

## _3.1. Wind turbine suitability model_

We used the 30,752 wind turbines in our study area to specify presence and absence of turbines within the 1 km[2 ] grid cells as our response variable in our model. We used these rotated values to parametrize our random forest model for predicting the probability of wind turbine suitability (Table 1, Fig. 3). ## **4. Discussion**

Wind energy will continue expanding across the United States given the pace of climate change and need to reduce greenhouse gas emission by 2030 (USDOE, 2008; Williams et al., 2015; Haley et al., 2019; United States Department of State and the United States Executive Office of the President, 2021). Our interests center on helping balance renewable energy development with environmental stewardship. Mitigating the potential negative impacts of wind facilities on wildlife requires identifying the locations most suitable for turbines and the potential significance these areas pose to species populations sharing these locations. We provide data identifying the locations with high suitability for turbine siting and wildlife, thereby describing potential conflict areas. Our intent is for wind development to proactively consider the conservation implications in these areas, helping developers provide renewable energy with reduced wildlife impacts (Diffendorfer et al., 2021; RuizGutierrez et al., 2021). We offer three case studies exemplifying the major types of wildlife and turbine conflict: bird mortality from turbine collisions (volitant long distance migratory, volitant resident migratory) and turbine avoidance (terrestrial resident). These cases demonstrate methodological examples for other species sharing similar life-history characteristics.

The simplest stage for minimizing conflicts between wind energy and wildlife is during siting (Allison et al., 2019). Our model predicting wind turbine suitability performed well with classification performance metrics and relatively high mean probability of wind turbine suitability (i.e., 65.7%) associated with new turbines and determined unbuilt sites. While our model predicted low wind turbine suitability associated with some new turbines and determined unbuilt sites, the utility to test the model’s predictive power and update the model as new turbines are built is a strength of our framework. Moreover, inclusion of new infrastructure and changes in landownership, and metrological conditions could further improve model predictions. The integration of species and habitat data demonstrates how conservation priorities can be established for species of concern that can conflict with wind energy. The exclusion layer can be used for planning to determine locations on the landscape that may likely never be developed for wind energy, but may contain suitable wind resources, so wind development has less impact on species and habitat in these areas.

Behavioral avoidance of wind infrastructure by whooping cranes occurs, causing habitat loss (Pearse et al., 2021). The Great Plains, the primary migration corridor for the Aransas Wood Buffalo Population, have some of the highest wind potential in the United States and have already seen substantial wind development and infrastructure in the last several decades (Fig. 3 this article, USDOE, 2008, Wiser et al., 2022). Although the Aransas Wood Buffalo Population is currently growing, continued population growth could be offset by adding new sources of anthropogenic mortality (Butler, Metzger et al., 2017). Our results show several areas of high conservation priority for whooping cranes due to the cooccurrence of high probability of wind turbine suitability and high intensity of use (Fig. 8A and 8B). ## _4.3. Lesser Prairie-Chickens_

There may be negative behavioral and demographic responses by prairie grouse to wind energy development including avoidance (i.e., displacement, causing habitat loss and fragmentation), or increased

predation from predatory raptors perching on overhead transmission lines (Pruett et al., 2009; Hagen, 2010; Hagen et al., 2011; Walters et al., 2014; Winder et al., 2014, 2015; Raynor et al., 2017; but see LeBeau et al., 2020; USFWS, 2021). Several studies document the influence of wind energy development on lesser prairie-chickens (Agha et al., 2020). Overall, it appears that population level impacts of wind energy on lesser prairie-chicken include avoidance-based habitat loss (USFWS, 2021).

We identified the Permian Basin in New Mexico as the highest conservation priority area for lesser prairie-chickens which is driven by the high probability of wind turbine suitability and the sand shinnery oak ecosystem supporting the highest population density of the species in the southern extent of their range (Fig. 9C and 9D). These areas are likely one of the most important strongholds for the species. Prudent conservation activities aimed at recognizing this stronghold while acknowledging future planning relating to wind development will help ensure habitat is maintained and restored to levels required to support population growth and colonization of restored habitat for the species. A promising strategy for lesser prairie-chickens, and other species of concern in general, could be siting wind energy facilities in altered habitats (e.g., already disturbed or developed areas) and outside of intact high-quality habitats, to abate impacts of energy development and operation (Diffendorfer et al., 2019; LeBeau et al., 2020).

We demonstrated that our predictive wind turbine suitability model establishes useful “species-wind turbine occurrence relationships” to identify conservation priorities on the landscape for proactive planning of wind development. Our integration of wind turbine suitability with biological and demographic modeling used a single species approach, to exemplify the framework. Planning wind energy to accommodate long distance migratory and resident species like whooping cranes and golden-eagles, or grassland obligate species such as the lesser prairiechicken, are anticipated to assist other imperiled species similarly impacted by wind development (Ward et al., 2020). While our model performed well, it did not account for socioeconomic factors, future but unbuilt transmission lines, private landowner decisions, setback agreements, local community politics, ordinances and opinions, and profit margins dictating the buildout of new wind turbines in suboptimal wind resource areas, as these factors are challenging to parametrize in a statistical framework. These shortcomings, leaves room for future improvements and as new turbines come online, our model can be and updated and validated to increase predictive accuracy.

wildlife species sensitive to wind energy development. We foresee our results forming a useful tool for informing landscape planning early in the siting process. Areas should be evaluated for the impacts of wind energy development to fully understand the population-level consequences of wind facilities to wildlife (May et al., 2019; Katzner et al., 2020). Methods developed from this study are transferable to other landscapes across the globe that are also experiencing increased renewable energy development. Our results should be used to site wind turbine facilities and supporting infrastructure in areas of high wind turbine suitability that are spatially coincident with places having low biological or ecological value.

## **5. Conclusions**

We developed a technique useful to avoid or minimize the negative impacts of wind development on wildlife which will hopefully support responsible clean energy development. While our application was demonstrated on biological data of three priority species there are many other data sources available of species occurrence and habitat distributions that could be integrated into our framework to better understand “species-wind turbine occurrence relationships”. Some of these data, for example, include GAP Analysis Program (Thomas et al., 2018), eBird data (Sullivan et al., 2014), the Movebank system (Kays et al., 2022), and Global Biodiversity Information Facility (https://www.gbif. org). Locations suitable for wind energy development will inevitably coincide with locations suitable for wildlife species of conservation concern. However, the environmental benefits of wind energy, ranging for substantial reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, air pollutants, and a reduced water use to electricity production ratio (Allison et al., 2019), are important and useful conservation advantages. In additional to the environmental benefits, economic incentives are extensive, including job creation, land lease revenue for private landowners, stimulus to local economies, and an increase in local tax base (AWEA, 2020; USDOE, 2022). The Great Plains is a region with much of the wind potential in the United States and several of the states in our study area (e.g., Colorado, Kansas, New Mexico) have rapidly increased wind generation (AWEA, 2020). The infrastructure, however, that comes with wind turbines, roads for installing and maintaining turbines, substations and transmission lines to store and transmit electricity to the power grid, can have negative impacts on some wildlife species. Collectively this creates a significant source of anthropogenic disturbance to wildlife populations and other environmental valuations, such as scenic views and recreation opportunities.
